title: India Moves to Bring Back Merchant Fees on UPI, Ending the Free-Transaction Era
excerpt: An amendment to India's payments law tabled in Parliament would create a legal basis for charging merchants on UPI transactions, potentially affecting the world's largest real-time payments network.
body:
• Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman tabled an amendment to India's Payment and Settlement Systems Act in Parliament on Tuesday, creating a legal basis for reintroducing a merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions.
  • No decision has been made on the level of fees, but reports suggest the charge would apply only to large merchants with annual turnover above ₹1-1.5 crore and transactions above ₹2,000.
  • UPI processed 23.6 billion transactions worth ₹29.9 trillion ($313.5 billion) in July 2026 alone, with PhonePe and Google Pay dominating the market.
  • Consumers and small merchants are expected to remain exempt from any fees.

India's free ride on UPI may be nearing its end. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman tabled an amendment to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act in Parliament on Tuesday that would allow the government to reintroduce a merchant discount rate on digital payments — a fee that was eliminated in 2022 to encourage adoption of cashless transactions.

The amendment removes the existing legal linkage between the Payment and Settlement Systems Act and the Income Tax Act, giving the central government the authority to designate which electronic payment methods remain exempt from charges. According to industry and regulatory sources cited by Reuters, the change creates a legal framework for charging an MDR on UPI, though no decision has been made on rates or implementation.

What the Numbers Look Like

UPI is, by transaction volume, one of the largest real-time payments networks in the world. In July 2026, the platform processed 23.6 billion transactions worth ₹29.9 trillion — roughly $313.5 billion. Walmart's PhonePe and Alphabet's Google Pay together dominate payments through the system.

Under the current zero-MDR regime, merchants pay nothing to accept UPI payments. Before 2022, they were charged an MDR of less than 1% of transaction value. Credit card transactions in India still carry an MDR of approximately 1.5%, and debit card transactions up to 0.9%.

Reports from the Economic Times and Livemint indicate the proposed MDR would apply only to merchants with annual turnover above ₹1 crore to ₹1.5 crore, and only on individual transactions exceeding ₹2,000. The rate could be set at 5-7 basis points, though the Payments Council of India had previously recommended 0.30%.

"There is a view that the model has to be commercially sustainable over time."

— Government source, as reported by Moneycontrol

Why the Industry Has Been Pushing for This

Payment companies and banks have been lobbying for the return of MDR for years. The zero-fee model eliminated a key revenue stream that funded the infrastructure behind UPI — the servers, security, and settlement systems that process billions of transactions monthly.

Industry executives have argued that without transaction-based revenue, payment firms cannot invest in expanding the ecosystem, particularly in smaller cities and rural areas. The government has partially compensated through direct subsidies, but these have not fully replaced the lost MDR revenue.

For fintech companies like MobiKwik, the return of MDR represents a new revenue stream. During its Q4 earnings call, MobiKwik co-founder Bipin Preet Singh said MDR on UPI transactions would be a new source of revenue for the company.

What It Means for Consumers and the Diaspora

The proposed changes explicitly target large merchants, not consumers. Roughly 90% of merchants accepting UPI payments fall within the small enterprise category and would remain exempt. According to government data, transactions of ₹2,000 and above account for only 4% of person-to-merchant UPI transactions, while 86% are below ₹500.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications are indirect but real. UPI has become the default payment method across India — the system that visitors use at restaurants, shops, and markets during trips home. If large merchants begin absorbing MDR costs, some may choose to pass them along through pricing, though consumer-facing surcharges are prohibited under current rules.

The broader concern is whether reintroducing fees, even at modest levels, could slow the adoption momentum that made UPI a global model for digital payments. India's zero-fee experiment proved that removing transaction costs could drive adoption at scale. The question now is whether the ecosystem has matured enough to sustain itself with fees reintroduced — or whether the government is betting that UPI's dominance is too entrenched to be disrupted by a few basis points.
nri_angle: UPI has become the primary way diaspora Indians send and receive money during visits home, and any fee changes affect the merchants and small businesses they transact with.
author: Diaspora Desk
